QF.id: AIFM CIII AIFs in India and Suitability_1

question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, CIO of Himalaya Arbitrage Fund, is drafting the PPM. Under SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012, which single feature BEST distinguishes a Category III AIF from Category I and Category II AIFs?

answer.text: It must invest primarily in unlisted securities of start-ups and early-stage ventures
It employs diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, including through listed or unlisted derivatives
It receives specific incentives or concessions from the government or regulators for being socially desirable
It is restricted to close-ended structures with a minimum tenure of 10 years

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Per SEBI (AIF) Regulations 2012, Category III AIF is defined as one that 'employs diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, including through investment in listed or unlisted derivatives.' Hedge funds fall here. This leverage + derivatives feature is what sets Cat III apart from Cat I (socially/economically desirable) and Cat II (no leverage, primarily unlisted). **The Trap:** Option A describes Cat I (Venture Capital/Angel/SME). Option C describes Cat I's policy rationale (concessions). Option D is wrong: Cat III uniquely PERMITS open-ended structures. Candidates often swap the categories. **Cross-Exam Context:** In XIX-D (Cat I/II Manager), the definition test centres on unlisted/early-stage focus. In XIX-B (Cat III Distributor), the same Cat III definition is tested but framed for selling. XIX-E tests it from the Manager's construction angle. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Lock this in: leverage + derivatives + complex strategies = Cat III. When designing a long-short or merger-arb book under the 2x leverage cap, you're squarely in Cat III territory — which is why fund-level MMR taxation, daily NAV, and HWM crystallisation all apply together.
